fraudguard_mapping.note: ML score >= 0.5 on FraudGuard's 0..1 anomaly scale
ML score >= 0.5 on FraudGuard's 0..1 anomaly scale

interpretation: Amount on its own carries almost no signal in this dataset: with FraudGuard's amount-based features and a population-wide baseline the model scores ROC-AUC 0.53 (0.5 is chance) and average precision 0.003, against 0.0017 for a random detector. Fraudulent and legitimate amounts overlap heavily, so a single baseline for everyone cannot separate them. On the dataset's 28 behavioural features the same algorithm reaches ROC-AUC 0.94 and average precision 0.152. Two conclusions follow. First, per-account baselines matter: FraudGuard compares each amount with that account's own spending history, which this anonymised dataset cannot provide. Second, the ML score is rightly a supporting signal (weight 0.30) next to explainable rules that use account history and location; richer features (device, merchant category, behaviour) would improve detection more than a different model would.
